text.p: These are some of the leading stories in Israeli newspapers on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
JERUSALEM POST
- Israel, Palestinian talks to resume in Israel on Thursday
- Israeli witnesses recount Naharayim murders.
- Prime Minister Netanyahu: Building of Jerusalem Jewish settlement and other settlements will continue.
- Israel El Al airlines resolves U.S. dispute.
- Israeli pharmaceutical giant Teva may move 120 research and development jobs abroad due to restrictive Israeli patent laws.
- Korea's Hanwha to open open office in Israel.
- Trade ministry refuses Israeli federation of chambres of commerce plea to drop ban on imports from Gulf states, saying such a move would "take a certain element of reciprocity".
YEDIOTH AHRONOTH
- Amazement in security establishment at army chief of staff's comments on possibility of Syrian surprise attack.
- Police to investigate ministers and members of parliament on connections with detained "Russian Mafia" figure.
- Bones removed from Jewish graves and set on fire in New York.
MAARIV
- Police to summon members of parliament to testify on connections with suspected "Russian Mafia" figure.
- Very senior government minister said in closed forum that two Jewish settlements in the Gaza Strip in the end will have to go to Palestinians.
- Finance minister on the bourse: I suggest that investors consider well and do everything with caution.
- High Court president shocked by conditions in Jerusalem lock-up; summons internal security minister for discussion.
- Unknown persons remove bodies from Jewish cemetery in New York and burn them.
HAARETZ
- Three ministers and five members of parliament will be questioned by police on connections with suspected "Russian Mafia" figure.
- Palestinian President Arafat met secretly in Amman with Iraqi ambassador to Jordan.
- Army officer: many soldiers evade army service in order not to serve in Lebanon.
- Israeli representative in San Francisco warns passing law against all conversions to Judaism other than those performed by Orthodox rabbis would hurt U.S. Jewish lobby.
